title: Toolkit: Cards and Templates for Payment Architecture Decisions

know: The sixteen cards and templates: payment state card, idempotency key card, webhook consumer contract, provider comparison card, funds-flow diagram template, reconciliation card, payout exception card, dispute evidence card, PCI scope card, routing rule card, platform liability card, onboarding requirement tracker, billing retry schedule card, peak plan, provider exit plan card and architecture decision record; the question each answers and the chapter that teaches it.
That every card asks for the same three things: the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception, and a date or deadline.
That the filled examples use Larkfield's fictional facts and are to be replaced, and that the provider comparison card is filled only from dated sources or 'Not public'.
can_do: Pick the card for the question on their desk, copy its fields and fill it with their own facts.
Start with the three cards the book's last chapter names (payment state, idempotency key, reconciliation) and say what each must contain for one money-moving call of their own.
Keep the cards current: review on a calendar, let incidents add fields, drop fields nobody reads.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a question from their own work, the reader picks the card that answers it and the chapter that teaches it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a nightly job that pays out to sellers sometimes times out and is re-run by hand, and last month 30 payouts came back from the receiving banks without anyone noticing for two weeks. Which two cards do you fill in first, which chapters teach them, and which three things does every card ask for?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The idempotency key card (idempotency-and-retries), for what key the payout call sends so that a re-run cannot pay twice; and the payout exception card (payouts-and-money-movement), for who is told when a payout is returned and by when it is resolved. Every card names the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader fills the idempotency key card correctly for a case the page does not contain.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: fill the idempotency key card for 'refund order 8841 in full' in a shop that lets support agents click Refund more than once. What is the key built from, what must it not be built from, and what do you do when the first call times out?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The key is derived from the business event, here the order and the refund's identity (order 8841, full refund, or the refund request's own id), so that every attempt for the same refund sends the same key. It is not a random value generated per attempt or per click. After a timeout the outcome is unknown: fetch the provider's record or retry with the same key; never send a new key.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sixteen cards, from a payment state card to a provider exit plan and an architecture decision record, each with the question it answers, its fields, a filled example and a link to the chapter that teaches it; the three things every card asks for (the record that is the truth, an owner, a date); which three to start with. Material: fictional Larkfield facts in the examples, to be replaced with the reader's own.

thesis.question: Which cards and templates do the chapters introduce, and what do the sixteen have in common that makes filling them worth a team's time?
thesis.claim: A team that cannot write down, for a recurring payment question, the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline has not yet decided that question, and the toolkit's sixteen cards force the decision before an incident does. Each card is introduced by the chapter that raises its question, from the payment state card ('what state is this payment in') through the idempotency key card, the webhook consumer contract and the reconciliation card to the provider exit plan card ('how would we leave this provider'), and each asks for those same three things.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a payment integration is already documented by its code, its provider dashboard and the provider's documentation, so that separate cards duplicate them and go stale, and that what a team left undecided is cheaper to learn from its first incident than to write down in advance.
thesis.so_what: A team fills three cards (payment state, idempotency key, reconciliation) for its own integration before its next release, and treats a blank owner or a blank deadline on any card as work to do now, not as a detail to settle after an incident.
thesis.how_why: Code and dashboards record what a system does when the answer arrives; they do not record who acts when it does not, and that is the case the book's failure patterns come from. Each card is the smallest form that forces the missing decision into writing. At Larkfield no document said what key a renewal retry must send, which system's record of a membership payment was the truth, or who owned a returned payout; the Double Charge, the Silent Webhook and the Payout That Bounced were found by members and studios first.

supporting_claims.claim: A recurring payment question leads through one table to the card that answers it and the chapter that teaches it.
Each card asks for the same three things, the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline, and is filled once with Larkfield's fictional facts.
The cards cite each other and meet at the payment state card and the reconciliation card, so a change to one says which others to re-read.

role.contribution: Gives the part the working records: one card per recurring question, so a decision taught in a chapter can be recorded without rereading it, and gives the book's closing takeaway its destination.

flow.rationale: The lookup table and the map of connections come first, because a reader arrives with a question and must find the card and see where it sits before reading any card. The sixteen cards then follow grouped by the part of the book whose chapter teaches them, in book order, so that a card can use the records of earlier ones: the payout exception and reconciliation cards use the states of the payment state card, the webhook contract moves those states, the exit plan card uses the routing rule and the PCI scope card. The decision record comes last because it changes rows on all the others. Moving the lookup behind the cards would make the page readable only front to back; the closing on upkeep needs all sixteen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A team that cannot write down the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date has not decided a payment question, and this page gathers sixteen cards that force that decision, each built from the chapter that raises its question.

The filled examples use Larkfield, the book's fictional studio-software platform, its 2027 Keel program of eight numbered decisions, K1 to K8, and its people, and the reader replaces every name, date and figure with their own.

conclusion.heading: Keeping the Cards True
conclusion.synthesis: The sixteen cards are one question asked sixteen times: which record counts as the truth, who acts when it disagrees with what the team believed, and by when. A card that no longer matches the system gives a wrong answer to all three with the same confidence.
conclusion.so_what: A stale card is worse than none because people trust its owner and its date, so the upkeep of the cards is part of the decision and three habits carry it.

callback.to: The opening statement that a team which cannot write down the record, the owner and the date has not decided the question.
callback.how: A card whose date has passed or whose owner has left is the same undecided question, written down.

takeaway.content: Fill the payment state card, the idempotency key card and the reconciliation card for one money-moving call before the next release; review every card on a calendar, let incidents add fields and drop fields nobody reads.

transition_in.introduces: How to keep them current.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three habits keep the cards current: review each on a calendar, let incidents add fields, and keep the set small.

open_questions: The plan and the journal spec say the chapters introduce these cards; only the provider comparison card is named as a card in a chapter (chapter 48), and the exit plan appears as the 'exit sheet' (chapter 22). Should chapters be edited to name their cards, or the journal spec to say the toolkit builds them from the chapters?

decision_log.decision: Kept the plan's sixteen cards. Fifteen are named as cards by no chapter (chapter 48 names the provider comparison card; chapter 22 calls the exit plan an 'exit sheet'), so each is built only from its chapter's 'In Practice at Larkfield' section and 'Questions to Ask', and the page says so per card.

decision_log.decision: Cards are separate sections in book order of their teaching chapter's part, as in ORDERED's toolkit; the part is a column of the lookup table. The provider exit plan card sits in Part X beside the comparison card, where chapter 50 tells the reader to keep it, with its fields from chapters 22 and 10. The decision record is last and is built from chapter 6's scene and chapter 10's Larkfield section.
